title: Stage 9: 500M users
scopeHtml: Scope: multi-region active-passive vs active-active, CAP per feature, conflict resolution, global routing, data residency. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Load and goal
notes.html:
Stage 9 goal: at 500M registered users spread across the world, Chirp must be fast for users everywhere and survive the loss of an entire region. One region means 150 to 300 ms round trips for users in India or Brazil, and one regional outage means total outage.

Quantity Value
Registered / DAU 500M / 200M
Split of DAU Americas 30%, Europe/Africa 25%, Asia-Pacific 45%
Timeline reads 4B/day = 46k/s avg, 140k/s peak
Posts 100M/day = 1,160/s avg, 3,500/s peak
Cross-region RTT US-East to EU about 80 ms, to Mumbai about 200 ms, to Singapore about 230 ms
Latency goal p95 timeline read under 300 ms for all users, so reads must be served in-region
Availability goal survive a region loss: RTO 5 min, RPO under 5 s for posts

Why speed of light matters. Light in fibre covers about 200 km per ms, so Mumbai to Virginia (13,000 km) is at least 65 ms one way, and real routes are about 100 ms. A page needing 4 sequential round trips costs 800 ms. Therefore the data has to be near the user, not just the CDN edge.

Industry examples. Facebook runs a primary region for writes with read replicas globally for TAO (the social graph cache); Instagram and Twitter used regional read replicas and later multi-primary designs; Netflix runs active-active in three AWS regions with the ability to evacuate one in minutes; Discord and Slack use cell/regional partitioning for tenants; DynamoDB global tables use last-writer-wins multi-region.

Everyday analogy. A global company opens local branch offices. Each branch handles its neighbours, and head office can step in if one branch burns down.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a CDN and calling it multi-region; CDNs cache static or public content, not personalised writes.
  • Ignoring that cross-region replication lag is real (typically 50 to 500 ms, can be seconds under load).

notes.title: Configuration
notes.html:
Regions. us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-south-1 (Mumbai) plus ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) as a fourth region once APAC load needs it. Each region is a full Stage 8 stack (3 AZs).

Layer Config
Global routing DNS latency-based routing (Route 53) with health checks; plus anycast IPs via AWS Global Accelerator or Cloudflare; TTL 30 to 60 s
User home region each user has home_region (stored in a global directory, replicated, 500M rows x 40 B = 20 GB) set at signup from country or ip
Posts store per region Postgres shards; a user's posts live in the home region (authoritative), async replicated to the other 2 regions for reads, replication lag target p99 < 2 s
Timeline cache regional Redis; fan-out workers in every region subscribe to a global stream of post events
Cross-region replication Kafka MirrorMaker 2 (or Confluent Cluster Linking) topic post.created, 48 partitions; or Postgres logical replication
Counters CRDT-style per-region counters (G-Counter): each region increments its own slot; sum on read
Session/auth JWT signed with a key distributed to all regions, 15 min access token, refresh token in regional store plus global revocation list in a small replicated store
Media S3 buckets per region with replication; CDN fronts all, origin shield per region 
# Route 53 style policy (sketch)
record: api.chirp.example
policy: latency
targets:
  - region: us-east-1   health_check: /readyz  weight: 100
  - region: eu-west-1   health_check: /readyz  weight: 100
  - region: ap-south-1  health_check: /readyz  weight: 100
failover:
  health_check_interval: 10s
  failure_threshold: 3        # 30 s to detect
  dns_ttl: 30s                # total ~60 to 90 s to shift

Per-feature consistency table (the CAP choices).

Feature Choice during a partition Reason
Login, passwords, payments CP: refuse in minority region or route to home wrong answer is worse than unavailable
Posting AP for the author: accept in home region; if home region down, queue locally (or fail over the home) users prefer to post
Timeline read AP: serve from local replica, maybe stale seconds
Follow/unfollow AP with last-writer-wins by timestamp, plus tombstones rare conflicts
Likes/retweet counts AP with CRDT counters approximate is fine
Username uniqueness CP: a global unique-index service or single-owner region cannot allow duplicates
Block/mute, account deletion CP-ish: must propagate; deletion needs a legal SLA safety
Search AP, regional index replicas

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "CAP says pick two": partitions are not optional; you pick between consistency and availability when one happens, per feature.
  • Forgetting the clock: last-writer-wins relies on timestamps; clock skew can drop the real latest write.

notes.title: Decision and why
notes.html:
1. Active-passive for the source of truth per user, active-active for reads and the stateless tier ("home region" model). Each user has exactly one writer region. That avoids multi-master conflicts for the biggest dataset (posts, graph edges owned by the follower) while every region serves reads and runs the full application. Facebook and Instagram use variants of this (a master region per shard, replicas elsewhere). It gives local read latency (about 40 ms server time + 20 ms to the user) and local write latency for most users, since a user's home region is the nearest.

2. Writes from a traveller. User from Mumbai flying to London: the request lands in eu-west-1, which forwards the write to Mumbai (about 100 ms) or accepts it into a local buffer and syncs. We use forwarding with read-your-writes: after a write, the client gets a min_version token (LSN or post id); reads from replicas wait or route to home until caught up. Sticky read-your-writes for 10 s.

3. Conflict resolution by data type.

  • Immutable events (posts): no conflict, id includes region bits.
  • Counters: CRDT G-counter / PN-counter.
  • Sets (followers): add-wins OR-Set or per-edge LWW with tombstone TTL 7 days.
  • Profile fields: last-writer-wins with hybrid logical clock (HLC) timestamps, since skew is bounded.
  • Anything with money or uniqueness: single owner region.

4. Global traffic routing: anycast for TCP/TLS termination near the user (shortens handshake RTTs), then latency-based routing to the closest healthy region; failover drain by reducing weight to 0 gradually (10% steps per minute) to avoid thundering herd on the survivor.

5. Data residency. GDPR, India DPDP, and similar laws may require storing personal data of EU users in the EU. Pin home_region of EU users to EU (not just nearest), keep personal data (email, phone, DMs) only there, and replicate only public content (posts) outward. Cross-region replicas of private data are not allowed. That constraint reduces failover choices: if EU fails, EU users go read-only or to another EU region (eu-central-1) as pair, not to the US.

Common interview traps.

  • Using hash of user id for home region and then discovering residency law.
  • Treating failover as automatic with no capacity: surviving region needs 50% spare headroom or load-shedding rules.

notes.title: Alternatives (branches)
notes.html:
Branch A: Multi-region topology

Active-passive Active-active (home region) Active-active (multi-master)
Write latency far users slow near for most near for all
Read latency replicas, fast fast fast
Failover promote standby, RTO 5 to 30 min, RPO secs users of failed region re-homed, RTO 1 to 5 min nothing to promote, instantly serves
Conflicts none rare (only travellers) frequent, need CRDT/LWW
Capacity cost standby idle (but paid) all regions used, need failover headroom same
Complexity low medium very high
Examples most banks, small SaaS Instagram/Facebook style, Slack cells Cassandra/Dynamo multi-DC, CockroachDB global tables, Spanner

Choose active-active with home region. Move to multi-master only for data types designed as CRDTs.

Branch B: Replication method

Postgres streaming (async) Logical + Kafka stream Distributed SQL (Spanner/Cockroach)
Granularity whole DB per table or topic automatic
Lag 100 ms to s 0.5 to 3 s commit-wait, 10 to 100 ms writes
Filtering for residency no yes with zone configs
Cost low medium high

Choose logical replication via Kafka because it allows residency filtering.

Branch C: Failover trigger

Fully automatic Human-approved Hybrid
Speed 1 to 2 min 10+ min 2 to 5 min
Risk of false positive (split brain) higher lower low

Choose hybrid: automatic traffic drain for a read-serving region; automatic write re-homing requires two independent signals (health checks and a quorum of observers from other regions) or an on-call click. Split brain (two writers for the same user) is worse than 5 min of read-only.

Branch D: Conflict handling

LWW CRDT Application merge / manual Avoid with single owner
Fits profile fields counters, sets docs uniqueness, money
Risk lost update design effort UX cost latency for travellers

Common interview traps.

  • Selecting active-active without naming the conflict strategy.
  • Failing over with stale replicas and not planning reconciliation of the lost 2 seconds of writes (keep the stream, replay).

notes.title: What breaks next
notes.html:
1. Cell size. Regions are huge failure domains with 100M+ users each; a bad deploy still takes a whole region (Stage 10 cells).
  2. Cross-region bandwidth cost, 3 regions replicating everything: tens of TB/day.
  3. Replication lag during bursts (celebrity event): followers in another region see the post 5 s later; need priority lanes for hot posts.
  4. Failover capacity: surviving regions need headroom; 3 regions at 66% each tolerates one loss, at 100% they do not.
  5. Operational skew: three different configurations drift. Infrastructure as code and region parity tests.
  6. Legal complexity: more countries means more residency rules (China, Russia, India often demand local presence).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing three regions give 3x capacity; to survive one loss you only get 2/3 usable at the same load targets.

notes.title: Cost
notes.html:
Approximate monthly (order of magnitude).

Item Monthly
Compute: three full regions, each about 1,000 nodes at ~$150 blended incl. DBs $450,000
Storage: 500M users x ~10 KB plus 100M posts/day x 300 B = 30 GB/day growth; 3 copies $80,000
Media storage 2.5 PB growth/year, tiered; replicated 3x $250,000
CDN egress: ~6 PB/month at about $0.02/GB blended after commit $120,000
Cross-region replication transfer: ~100 TB/month x $0.02 $2,000 (small for text; media is the big one: add $30,000)
Global Accelerator, DNS, observability multi-region $60,000
Failover headroom (33% over base) included above, about $150,000 of it
Total about $1.0 to 1.3M/month, $2 to $2.6 per 1,000 registered users

Going multi-region typically multiplies infrastructure by 2.5 to 3x relative to a single region at the same traffic.

Common interview traps.

  • Replicating all media to all regions; replicate only on demand (pull-through origin shield) for the long tail.

notes.title: LLD view
notes.html:
enum Region { US, EU, APAC }

record UserHome(UserId id, Region home, boolean euResident) {}

interface HomeDirectory { UserHome of(UserId id); }  // global, cached 5 min

class PostService {
    Post create(UserId author, String text, ReadYourWritesToken ryw) {
        UserHome h = dir.of(author);
        if (h.home() != self) return forwarder.forward(h.home(), author, text); // traveller
        Post p = repo.insert(snowflake.next(self), author, text);
        events.publish(new PostCreated(p));        // mirrored to other regions
        ryw.advance(p.id());                       // client pins reads for 10 s
        return p;
    }
}

// G-counter CRDT for likes
class GCounter {
    private final long[] slots = new long[3];      // per region
    void inc(Region r) { slots[r.ordinal()]++; }
    long value() { return Arrays.stream(slots).sum(); }
    void merge(GCounter o) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) slots[i] = Math.max(slots[i], o.slots[i]); }
}

Snowflake ids reserve 3 bits for region so ids remain unique without coordination. Hybrid logical clock: max(local_physical, last_seen) + counter keeps ordering monotone across skewed clocks.

Common interview traps.

  • Using wall-clock System.currentTimeMillis() for LWW across regions without HLC.
  • Making the home-directory lookup a synchronous cross-region call on every request; cache it and replicate.

notes.title: Decision gravity
notes.html:
Decision Gravity Why
Home-region ownership model One-way door All data, ids, residency and failover are built on it
Region count and locations Semi-reversible Adding a region is a project, removing is easier
Region bits in ids One-way door Embedded everywhere
Replication via Kafka vs native Reversible-ish Plumbing
CRDT counters Reversible with migration Data format change
Residency pinning One-way (legal) Moving EU data out is forbidden
DNS TTL / failover thresholds Reversible Config
Choosing Spanner-like DB One-way Engine change

Common interview traps.

  • Not distinguishing the legal one-way door (data location) from technical ones.

notes.title: Concepts learned
notes.html:
• Latency physics and why multi-region
  • Active-passive vs active-active vs multi-master
  • Home-region ownership; read-your-writes tokens
  • CAP and PACELC applied per feature
  • LWW, HLC, CRDTs (G-counter, OR-set), conflict policy by data type
  • Latency-based DNS, anycast, failover drain
  • Data residency and sovereignty
  • Split brain and failover capacity

Common interview traps.

  • Using "eventual consistency" without saying how convergence is guaranteed.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• At 500M users, users everywhere need local reads; use 3 regions each with a full Stage 8 stack.
  • Each user has one home region that owns writes (active-active at the regional level, single-writer per user), so conflicts are rare.
  • Choose CAP per feature: login and uniqueness are CP; timelines, likes and follows are AP with CRDTs or LWW (HLC).
  • Route with anycast and latency-based DNS, drain failed regions gradually, keep human or quorum approval before re-homing writes.
  • Data residency pins personal data to a legal region.
  • Cost is roughly 2.5 to 3x a single region: about $1.0 to 1.3M/month.
